title: Spread (prison food)
wikitext:
{{Short description|Meal made by prison inmates}}
A '''spread''' is a prison meal made by inmates. Spreads are often made with [[Prison commissary|commissary]] ingredients, such as [[Instant noodle|instant ramen]] and [[corn puffs]]. Spreads can be simple meals, or elaborate and inventive combinations of ingredients. Spreads may be used to supplement or replace the government-mandated meals provided to prisoners by the prison, due to the unpalatable and insubstantial nature of many prison meals.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cate|first=Sandra|date=2008-08-01|title="Breaking Bread with a Spread" in a San Francisco County Jail|url=https://online.ucpress.edu/gastronomica/article-abstract/8/3/17/47468/Breaking-Bread-with-a-Spread-in-a-San-Francisco?redirectedFrom=fulltext|journal=Gastronomica|language=en|volume=8|issue=3|pages=17–24|doi=10.1525/gfc.2008.8.3.17|issn=1529-3262|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Purpose and history ==
The preparation and consumption of evening "spreads" can be a social bonding experience. Although the term "spread" was coined in US prisons, similar improvised meals are made in prisons around the world, including in the United Kingdom and many Asian countries.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=The Art of Gourmet Cooking in Prison|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/the-art-of-gourmet-cooking-in-prison-511/|access-date=2021-07-31|website=Vice.com|language=en}}</ref>

A study on self-catering in Danish prisons found that being able to make choices and exercise responsibility regarding their foods had a positive impact on prisoners. The study concluded that the ability to prepare their own food according to personal preferences and cultural affinity could have a positive impact on prisoners' social re-integration after prison.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kjaer Minke|first=Linda|date=2014|title=Cooking in prison--from crook to cook|journal=International Journal of Prisoner Health|volume=10|issue=4|pages=228–238|doi=10.1108/IJPH-09-2013-0044|issn=1744-9219|pmid=25764291}}</ref>

=== United States ===
The importance of spread and other commissary foods has led to the use of ramen as a currency in some prisons in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ramen Noodles Are Now The Prison Currency Of Choice|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2016/08/26/491236253/ramen-noodles-are-now-the-prison-currency-of-choice|access-date=2021-07-31|website=NPR.org|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=In Prison, Sharing Ramen Can Be More Powerful Than Gang Affiliation|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/in-prison-sharing-ramen-can-be-more-powerful-than-gang-affiliation/|access-date=2021-07-31|website=Vice.com|language=en}}</ref> The [[Michigan Department of Corrections]] reported that ramen was the most sold commissary item in 2016, ahead of coffee, rice, soap and razors.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Cardinale|first=Alexandra|date=2018-11-14|title=Why ramen is so valuable in prison|url=https://www.vox.com/the-goods/2018/11/14/18052246/ramen-prison-valuable|access-date=2021-07-31|website=Vox|language=en}}</ref> A 2016 study of a male state prison in the United States indicated that [[Top Ramen]] noodles were one of the most valuable prison commodities, due to the declining quality and quantity of food in many prisons.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2016-08-23|title=Ramen noodles 'are most valuable US prison commodity', study suggests|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-37162373|access-date=2021-07-31}}</ref> Diminished access to commissary food during the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United States|COVID-19 pandemic]] has caused inmates in some prisons to have anxiety over their ability to obtain adequate food.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Food In Prison|url=https://impactjustice.org/impact/food-in-prison/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://impactjustice.org/wp-content/uploads/IJ-Eating-Behind-Bars-Release1.pdf|archive-date=July 31, 2021|archive-format=PDF|access-date=2021-07-31|website=Impact Justice|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Preparation ==
[[File:Instantnoodles.jpg|alt=A brick of uncooked instant ramen noodles on a wooden table|thumb|Typical instant noodles used in prison spreads]]
Spreads are often created using ingredients purchased from prison commissaries or saved from meals provided by the prison. Prisoners are forced to use substitutes for cooking appliances and tools due to prison safety regulations. Common substitutions include [[hot plate]]s which do not reach [[boiling point]] in place of stoves, and ID cards in place of knives or other cutting tools.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Camplin|first=Erika|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=am1xDQAAQBAJ&dq=spread+food+prison&pg=PA81|title=Prison Food in America|date=2016-12-08|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-1-4422-5348-3|pages=82|language=en}}</ref> Some prisoners create heating elements  by improvising a "stinger" by using electricity and metal nail clippers to heat up a pot of water.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Fine Art of Cooking in Prison|url=https://www.thrillist.com/eat/nation/the-fine-art-of-cooking-in-prison-ingenious-jailhouse-cooking-hacks|access-date=2021-07-31|website=Thrillist|language=en}}</ref>

== Variations and ingredients ==
The base ingredient for most spreads is cooked instant ramen noodles, to which other ingredients are added for flavor and nutritional value.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2016-08-24|title=Cooking with ramen: Prisoners get creative|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-37164279|access-date=2021-07-31}}</ref> Shelf stable snack ingredients like [[Pork rind#United States|pork rinds]], [[corn puff]]s, [[drink mix]]es and canned tuna are often combined into improvised recipes. Some dishes are approximations of common meals enjoyed by inmates such as [[dumpling]]s, [[tamale]]s, or soups, while others are more experimental.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Behind Bars, Cheap Ramen Is As Good As Gold|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2015/11/04/454671629/behind-bars-cheap-ramen-is-as-good-as-gold|access-date=2021-07-31|website=NPR.org|language=en}}</ref> Inmates are limited in the ingredients available to them because of the expense of commissary food, often relying on money sent from relatives outside of prison.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Genis|first=Daniel|date=2014-06-21|title=Tales of a Jailhouse Gourmet: How I learned to Cook in Prison|language=en|work=The Daily Beast|url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2014/06/21/tales-of-a-jailhouse-gourmet-how-i-learned-to-cook-in-prison|access-date=2021-07-31}}</ref>
